opus-5.5.text:
Meituan is one of the more interesting surprises in the Chinese open-model ecosystem. A lot of people in the West hadn't heard of them, and then the LongCat models showed up as a serious open-weight release. They're big mixture-of-experts models with real technical reports and some genuinely novel architecture choices. That told me the team isn't just fine-tuning someone else's base model. They're doing frontier-style pretraining in-house.

On prospects, I'd break it into a few pieces.

**Talent and compute.** Meituan is a huge, profitable consumer company, so they can afford the GPUs and the researchers. In China right now, having the compute and the willingness to spend is a big part of the battle. They've shown they can execute on large-scale training, which is not trivial.

**Strategic fit.** This is where it gets more interesting than a pure lab like DeepSeek or Moonshot. Meituan has an enormous local-services business: food delivery, travel, in-store commerce. That's a natural home for agents. If you believe the next phase is models that take actions on your behalf, like ordering, booking, and coordinating, Meituan has the distribution and the real-world plumbing that most labs would kill for. So their models don't have to be the absolute best on every benchmark. They need to be very good and deeply integrated into products people already use daily.

**Open weights.** Releasing openly is a smart play for them. It builds credibility, attracts researchers, and makes them part of the conversation alongside Qwen, DeepSeek, and others. Chinese companies have basically set the pace in open models over the last year or so, and Meituan joining that wave reinforces that China's open ecosystem is broad, not just one or two labs.

**The risks.** It's a crowded field. Alibaba, ByteDance, Tencent, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu, MiniMax: everyone is shipping. Staying near the frontier means continuous, expensive investment, and the half-life of any model's lead is a few months. The question for Meituan is whether leadership stays committed when the payoff is more about long-term agentic products than near-term revenue. Export controls and access to top-end chips are a constraint for everyone there too.

Overall, I'm fairly bullish that they'll remain a credible player. I'm less sure they become *the* defining lab. Their best outcome is probably owning the "AI that actually gets things done in your daily life" layer in China. That's a very valuable position even without topping the leaderboards.

r001.rationale: The response is bullish on Meituan’s prospects, but it does not predict that companies entering the AI business early will probably do well.

r002.rationale: It describes potential value from integrating models into daily services, but does not predict substantial market demand for intelligence sold by AI companies.

fable-5.1.text:
Meituan is one of the more interesting cases to me, honestly, because it doesn't fit the mold of what people expected a frontier-ish Chinese lab to look like. It's a food delivery and local services company. A year or two ago, if you'd asked me which Chinese companies would be putting out competitive open models, I'd have said Alibaba with Qwen, maybe DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu. I would not have said Meituan.

But then LongCat showed up, and the models were genuinely decent. Not state of the art, but solidly in the pack, with reasonable training reports and an open license. And that tells you a couple of things.

First, the barrier to entry for a very large model has come down a lot in China specifically. The playbook is pretty well understood now. DeepSeek basically published the recipe for efficient mixture-of-experts training, Qwen has shown how to do the data and post-training work at scale, and there's a deep pool of engineers who've cycled through those organizations. If you have a few thousand GPUs and a budget line that a company of Meituan's size can absorb, you can get to a credible model in under a year. That was not true in 2023.

Second, the motivation is a little different from the American companies. Meituan isn't trying to sell API tokens to the world. They have an enormous operational business, with hundreds of millions of users, logistics, merchant tooling, and customer service, and a lot of that is text and decision-making that a model can touch. So the way I'd frame it is: they're building infrastructure for their own business first, and the open releases are partly recruiting, partly reputation, and partly a way to stay in the conversation so they aren't dependent on a competitor like Alibaba for their core AI stack. That's a very rational thing to do if you're a big Chinese internet company and you watch ByteDance and Alibaba both go all-in.

Where I'm more skeptical is on whether they can sustain being at the frontier. The thing that separates the labs that stick around from the ones that put out one or two good models and then fade is the willingness to keep spending when the returns to the core business aren't obvious yet. Meituan's margins are under real pressure, there's a brutal delivery price war going on, and the capital for training runs competes directly with that. If I had to bet, I'd say they'll stay a solid second-tier open model producer, with models that are useful and well-engineered, but I don't expect them to be the ones pushing the Pareto frontier the way DeepSeek or Qwen do.

The broader point, and this is the thing I keep coming back to, is that the Chinese open model ecosystem now has something like six or eight serious players, and Meituan being one of them is a sign of how deep the bench is. In the US, we have basically Meta, which has pulled back, and a handful of smaller efforts. So even if Meituan individually isn't a frontier lab, the fact that a food delivery company can plausibly do this is itself the story.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Meituan’s prospects and predicts it may remain a solid second-tier model producer, but does not predict that companies entering AI early will probably do well.

r002.rationale: The response says Meituan is not trying to sell API tokens broadly and emphasizes internal business uses; it makes no claim about substantial market demand for intelligence sold by AI companies.

astra-6.text:
I’d be cautious about making a strong prediction without knowing more about their models and strategy. But I’d separate two questions: can Meituan build a competitive language model, and can it turn language models into a valuable part of its business? Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

If they have tasks where a model can reliably improve the customer experience or reduce costs, they could get a lot of value without having the best model on every benchmark. The harder question is whether training their own models gives them enough of an advantage over adapting models that are already available.

So I’d look for evidence of useful deployment: are people using it, does it work reliably, and do the economics make sense? That would tell me more about their prospects than the size of the investment alone.

r001.rationale: The response is cautious about Meituan’s prospects and does not predict that companies entering AI early will probably succeed.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible business value from model deployment but does not predict substantial market demand for intelligence sold by AI companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: can Meituan build a strong language model, and can it turn language models into a valuable product? Those are related, but they’re different bets.

On the product side, there’s a plausible opportunity. If you can help people find what they want, make recommendations more useful, or give merchants better tools, you have ways to create value without having the best model on every benchmark.

The harder question is whether investing heavily in a frontier model gives them an advantage over using models available elsewhere. That takes a lot of resources, and you need a clear reason why owning that capability matters to your business. So I’d be interested in how closely their model work connects to actual products. I wouldn’t make a confident prediction about their prospects from the investment alone.

r001.rationale: It discusses Meituan’s possible product opportunities and the costs of building a frontier model, but does not predict that companies entering AI early will probably do well.

r002.rationale: It identifies ways language models could create value for Meituan, but does not predict substantial market demand for intelligence sold by AI companies.
